title: Bastionless on-prem inference network patterns and DNS/egress playbook
content:
Purpose and context:
This note documents a lightweight, "bastionless" network pattern for on‑prem / VPC private inference installs where customers prefer minimal jump hosts and strict egress control. The audience is SEs and customers evaluating Redwood Private where compliance teams want no open management ports from the Internet and security teams want clear egress and DNS handoff patterns.

Goals:
- Avoid persistent bastion/jump hosts for operational access where possible.
- Provide predictable egress flows for telemetry, model downloads, and optional hosted-control-plane callbacks.
- Keep DNS resolution deterministic for private endpoints (console, model registry) while supporting customer firewall policies.
- Minimize required customer firewall changes and present fallback options (proxy, egress appliance, or S3/RP sync) for strict environments.

Constraints we often see from customers:
- No inbound 22/3389 from Internet allowed; management must be via private network or ephemeral tunnels.
- Egress-only allowed to a fixed set of IPs or through a corporate proxy.
- DNS must be managed on-prem; split-horizon DNS is common.
- Customers may require mTLS or IP allowlists for control-plane traffic.
- Air‑gapped customers may only allow pull of artifacts via an approved artifact repo.

High-level pattern options (ranked by customer friction):
1) Egress via corporate HTTP forward proxy (preferred):
   - All outbound HTTPS goes through customer proxy. Redwood components make outbound TLS connections to our control plane and to model artifact hosts (optionally mirrored to internal registry).
   - No inbound firewall openings required.
   - DNS: internal resolver returns private IPs for redwood-internal domains or proxy resolves externally.
   - Pros: least invasive, fits enterprise visibility and DLP.
   - Cons: requires proxy support for large downloads and possibly SNI/CONNECT passthrough tuning.

2) Egress to a short allowlist of static IP ranges owned by Redwood:
   - Customer opens egress to our IP ranges and optionally to specific ports (443, 123 for NTP).
   - DNS: customer can use corporate resolver or forward to public resolver for Redwood domains.
   - Pros: simple for customers who can open a few CIDR blocks.
   - Cons: some customers don't allow any outbound to external IPs.

3) Mirror/artifact-sync via customer-hosted registry (air‑gap friendly):
   - Redwood provides tooling to mirror model artifacts to a customer registry (S3, Artifactory, Nexus) or a remote blob store accessible from the private network via internal endpoints.
   - Control-plane operations can be completely offline; updates via scheduled syncs initiated from within the customer's environment.
   - DNS: fully internal.
   - Pros: fits highest-security customers.
   - Cons: higher operational overhead and slower model updates.

Bastionless access model (patterns):
- Admin operations are performed over one of the following:
  a) Privileged admin pod running an ephemeral web shell accessible only from an internal admin subnet + short-lived service account credentials.
  b) CI/CD runner inside customer network (GitHub Actions self-hosted, GitLab runner) that runs ops playbooks against local control plane APIs.
  c) Short‑lived outbound SSH tunnels initiated by an operator VM (jump out) to an approved Redwood maintenance endpoint using mutual TLS and ephemeral certificates (audit logged).
- Do not require inbound management ports on inference nodes.

DNS strategy recommendations:
- Split‑horizon with internal authoritative entries for the Redwood control plane and registry hostnames is preferred. Example: redwood-control.company.internal resolves to an internal VIP that terminates TLS at the local control plane router.
- If split‑horizon isn't possible, recommend customers use their HTTP proxy to resolve or forward DNS queries for specific Redwood domains to an external resolver. Document the FQDNs that must resolve: control-plane.redwood.ai, models.redwood.ai, metrics.redwood.ai, signing.redwood.ai.
- SNI & TLS: Redwood supports SNI-based routing; ensure customer proxies/NGINX allow SNI passthrough for CONNECT. If the proxy terminates TLS, mutual TLS must be configured between customer proxy and internal services.

Egress details and recommendations:
- Required outbound ports: 443 (HTTPS), 123 (NTP) optional, 853 (DoT) optional.
- Prefer hostnames over IP allowlisting when possible. If customer requires IPs, provide a signed list of IP prefixes and a weekly delta notification.
- Larger model downloads should be chunked and support HTTP Range requests; recommend customers allow sustained connections for large content or configure caching reverse proxies (e.g., AWS S3 VPC endpoint or on-prem CDN edge).
- For telemetry/metrics: allow batched outbound HTTPS to metrics endpoints; provide a low‑traffic telemetry mode for highly restricted networks.

Ingress (serving) considerations:
- For private inference endpoints exposed to customer applications, the recommended pattern is an internal NLB/ALB fronting the inference pool within the customer VPC.
- Use mTLS between customer app and inference endpoint when isolation is required. Support client certs via our SDK or sidecar.
- If customer needs cross-account access, use VPC peering or transit gateway with restricted routes for inference subnets only. Avoid public DNS advertise for inference endpoints.

Network security & firewall rules (example minimal):
- Control plane node (private): allow inbound from internal admin subnets, allow outbound to customer proxy or Redwood CIDRs. Block inbound 0.0.0.0/0 on management ports.
- Inference nodes: allow inbound from internal app subnets only (application port e.g., 443/TLS), allow outbound to internal registry and to the control plane.
- Bastionless admin: restrict access to ephemeral admin pods via kube‑rbac and short token TTLs; log all execs to central SIEM.

Operational playbook (quick steps for SE run):
1) Determine customer's egress policy: proxy / allowlist / air‑gap.
2) Map required FQDNs and check DNS behavior (internal resolver, forwarders).
3) If proxy: provide proxy config template and test with curl --proxy and SNI passthrough checks.
4) If allowlist: provide IPs and port list; validate with tcpdump from a test node.
5) If mirror: coordinate artifact sync cadence and provide scripts.
6) Deploy with admin access pattern chosen (ephemeral pod or CI runner).
7) Run health checks: TLS handshake checks, DNS resolution tests, artifact fetch tests, and model load tests.

Test cases to include in customer POC:
- DNS split horizon verification (resolve control-plane domain from private subnets).
- Proxy CONNECT + SNI passthrough test for large artifact download.
- mTLS handshake from sample client to inference endpoint.
- Artifact mirror workflow, validate checksum and model load.
- Failure mode: simulate proxy outage and validate retry/backoff and cached artifacts behavior.

Open questions & follow-ups for Engineering:
- Can the agent support more aggressive chunked downloads to be friendlier to proxy caches? (ask artifact team)
- Provide a signed, short‑lived certificate workflow for ephemeral outbound tunnels (security team).
- Create a telemetry low bandwidth mode for constrained networks.

Action items for SEs (owner in parentheses):
- Draft proxy config template and test harness (Ethan).
- Add artifact-sync example repo for S3/NFS mirror (Jin).
- Produce IP prefix change notification cadence and signed list format (Samir).
- Create an internal KB with curl/test commands and expected responses (Priya).

Appendix: quick command snippets
- DNS check: dig @10.0.0.2 control-plane.redwood.ai +short
- Proxy CONNECT + SNI test: curl -v --proxy http://proxy:3128 https://control-plane.redwood.ai/health -H "Host: control-plane.redwood.ai"
- mTLS test using openssl: openssl s_client -connect inference.vpc.internal:443 -cert client.pem -key client.key -servername inference.vpc.internal

Notes to self: keep this playbook small and modular; customers want a 30‑minute checklist they can hand to infra teams and an optional deeper doc for security reviewers.

End of note.
